findings.claim: Atoms are incredibly small — about 0.1 nanometres across.
findings.truth: 0.1 nm is the atomic RADIUS, not the width. AQA states the radius of an atom is about 0.1 nm (1 x 10-10 m), so the diameter is about 0.2 nm.
findings.evidence: spec 4.1.1.5: 'Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 x 10-10 m).'

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'What is the approximate diameter of a typical atom?' answered 'About 0.1 nanometres.'
findings.truth: 0.1 nm is the radius. The card teaches the spec value under the wrong quantity.

findings.claim: Practice question typed '9 marks — Evaluate' with a 7-9 / 4-6 / 1-3 band ladder.
findings.truth: AQA GCSE Chemistry 8462 papers use multiple choice, structured, closed short answer and open response; the extended open response is a 6-mark item. There is no 9-mark question format.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Assessments (Paper 1: 1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks, Foundation and Higher Tier)

findings.claim: Practice question typed '12 marks + 4 SPaG — Extended' with a 9-12 band and four spelling and grammar marks.
findings.truth: AQA GCSE Chemistry 8462 has no 12-mark question and awards no marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. The longest item is a 6-mark open response.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Assessments; no SPaG allocation appears anywhere in the assessment section

findings.claim: 'A sodium atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. Calculate the number of protons, neutrons and electrons' typed as 6 marks, with 'Clear working shown (1 mark)' and 'Correct final answers (1 mark)' padding the scheme.
findings.truth: The task has three answers, so it is a 3-mark calculation. Marks are not given twice for the same working.
findings.evidence: spec 4.1.1.5 (calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons); mark plausibility

findings.claim: Group 1 elements 'have lower melting points and higher densities going down the group'.
findings.truth: Melting point does fall down Group 1. Density mostly rises, but potassium is less dense than sodium, so the blanket claim can mislead. The spec does not require a Group 1 density trend.
findings.evidence: spec 4.1.2.5 (Group 1: reactivity, outer shell, predict from given trends)

findings.claim: 'One _____ equals 1000 cm3.' options dm3 / m3 / mm3 / litre, correct = dm3.
findings.truth: 'litre' is also correct: 1 litre = 1000 cm3, and the lesson itself says 1 dm3 = 1000 cm3 = 1000 ml = 1 litre. A student picking litre is marked wrong. Replace the distractor.
findings.evidence: lesson content n23; settled unit fact

findings.claim: Moles, molar mass, reacting masses and mol/dm3 concentration questions carry no tier flag, although the article hides the same material behind higher-only wrappers.
findings.truth: In 8462, 4.3.2.1 Moles, 4.3.2.2 Amounts of substances in equations, 4.3.2.4 Limiting reactants and 4.3.4 Concentrations in mol/dm3 are all (HT only). Foundation students should be told to skip them. Concentration in g/dm3 (4.3.2.5) stays at both tiers and is left unflagged.

findings.claim: Knowledge checks on Avogadro's constant, mol/dm3 units, the moles equation and the mol / mol dm-3 match carry no tier flag.
findings.truth: All four sit in (HT only) sections of 8462. Flag them so a Foundation student knows to skip.

findings.claim: Ten of the thirteen flashcards drill HT-only moles work with no tier flag.
findings.truth: Flag the HT-only cards. The cm3 to dm3 conversion, the 1 dm3 cloze and the g/dm3 concentration card stay at both tiers and are left alone.

findings.claim: 'The most reactive metals (potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium) react vigorously with water and acids.'
findings.truth: Aluminium does not react vigorously with water, and magnesium reacts with cold water only very slowly. Grouping them with potassium, sodium and calcium teaches the 'all reactive metals react with water' misconception. Lithium also belongs in the top group.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1.2 (reactions of potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron and copper with water or dilute acids, at room temperature); settled chemistry

findings.claim: Key-fact reactivity series 'K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, C, Zn, Fe, H, Cu, Ag, Au' omits lithium.
findings.truth: The spec names lithium as one of the metals students must place in order, between sodium and calcium.

findings.claim: The unwrapped key fact and the conclusion give oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons to both tiers, while the article hides the same electron material behind a higher-only wrapper.
findings.truth: Loss and gain of OXYGEN is both-tier (4.4.1.1, 4.4.1.3). Oxidation and reduction in terms of ELECTRONS is 4.4.1.4 (HT only). Keep both, but flag the electron version.

findings.claim: Strong and weak acids appear unflagged in the conclusion, a practice question, a knowledge check and three flashcards, although the article gates the same material behind a higher-only wrapper.
findings.truth: 4.4.2.6 Strong and weak acids is (HT only) in 8462. Flag the questions and the takeaway.

findings.claim: 'Required Practical 4 involves electrolysing aqueous solutions using inert electrodes.'
findings.truth: In AQA GCSE Chemistry 8462 the electrolysis of aqueous solutions is required practical 3. Required practical 4 is the investigation of temperature changes in reacting solutions. This is leftover Combined Science numbering.
findings.evidence: spec 8.2.3 Required practical activity 3 (electrolysis) and 8.2.4 Required practical activity 4 (temperature changes)

findings.claim: Aluminium oxide is defined as 'the ore from which aluminium is extracted', in the glossary as well.
findings.truth: Aluminium oxide is a purified compound, not an ore. The lesson's own definition of an ore is a rock from which a metal can be extracted economically.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1.3 (ores are compounds found in the Earth) and 4.4.3.3; internal consistency with lesson 6

findings.claim: A flashcard asks the student to write the cathode half-equation for molten lead bromide, but the article hides every half-equation behind a higher-only wrapper.
findings.truth: Writing half equations throughout section 4.4.3 is (HT only). Flag the card.

findings.claim: The bond-energy calculation question and two flashcards on the energy-change formula carry no tier flag, although the article gates the calculation behind a higher-only wrapper.
findings.truth: 4.5.1.3 The energy change of reactions is (HT only). The arithmetic in the question is correct (679 - 864 = -185 kJ/mol, exothermic); only the tier flag is missing.

findings.claim: The qualitative bond model runs through the lesson with no tier gate: 'more energy is released when new bonds form than is needed to break the original bonds' (n5, n9), 'Bond breaking is always an endothermic process' (n18), the balance rule (n19), the fourth takeaway, knowledge check 4 and practice question 6.
findings.truth: All of that is 4.5.1.3, which 8462 heads (HT only); 4.5.1.1 is limited to measuring temperature change and says calculation of energy changes is not required. Options: (a) wrap n17-n19 and re-word the takeaway, knowledge check and question 6, which strips the mechanism from the Foundation lesson and leaves exothermic/endothermic as bare definitions; (b) leave the prose and flag only the calculation, as done for F18; (c) ask AQA-style: many centres teach the qualitative bond model to Foundation as background. Recommend (b) plus a Foundation-safe re-word of takeaway 4 only if Tom wants strict gating.
findings.evidence: spec 4.5.1.1 ('Limited to measurement of temperature change. Calculation of energy changes or delta H is not required.') vs 4.5.1.3 (HT only)

findings.claim: This nine-lesson unit is built from the Combined Science lessons and omits the chemistry-only (separate science) content that AQA 8462 examines on Paper 1.
findings.truth: Missing or barely covered: 4.1.3 Properties of transition metals (only a short collapsible in lesson 2, no coloured compounds / variable ion charges / catalysis detail against Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu); 4.2.4 Bulk and surface properties including nanoparticles (nanoscience 1-100 nm, PM2.5 and PM10 sizes, surface area to volume ratio, uses and risks) - entirely absent; 4.3.3 Percentage yield and atom economy - entirely absent; 4.3.5 Volumes of gases, molar volume 24 dm3 at RTP (HT only) - entirely absent; 4.4.2.5 Titrations and required practical 2 (strong acid with strong alkali, HT concentration calculation) - entirely absent; 4.5.2 Chemical cells, batteries and hydrogen fuel cells - entirely absent. The sibling science-aqa unit carries lessons 10-12 on transition metals and nanoparticles, yield and atom economy and gas volumes, and titrations and cells; those belong here. Recommend porting or building three lessons rather than editing the nine.

findings.claim: Required practical coverage: only required practical 1 (lesson 7, correctly numbered) and required practical 3 (lesson 8, after the F15 fix) are named.
findings.truth: Required practical 4, the investigation of variables affecting temperature changes in reacting solutions, sits in topic 5 and is never named in lesson 9. Required practical 2, the titration, is absent with the rest of the titration content (see F20).

findings.claim: Lesson 5 is tiered 'both', but four of its six sections are inside higher-only wrappers.
findings.truth: In 8462 almost all of the moles content is (HT only). The gating in the article is correct; after the F8-F10 flags, a Foundation student sees only concentration in g/dm3 and the unit conversions. Tom may prefer to retier the lesson H, or to move the g/dm3 material into lesson 7.

findings.claim: Checker brief anchor: '8462 assesses moles / reacting masses / concentration in mol/dm3 at BOTH tiers unlike Trilogy'.
findings.truth: The spec does not support this. In 8462, 4.3.2.1 Moles, 4.3.2.2 Amounts of substances in equations, 4.3.2.3 Using moles to balance equations, 4.3.2.4 Limiting reactants and 4.3.4 Concentrations in mol/dm3 are all headed (HT only). The existing higher-only wrappers were therefore kept, not removed.

summary: Nine lessons checked against AQA GCSE Chemistry 8462. Every equation, half equation and worked example recomputed and correct. Three HIGH errors: 0.1 nm taught as the atom's width rather than its radius, a 9-mark and a 12-mark-plus-SPaG question format that this paper does not use, and the electrolysis required practical numbered 4 instead of 3. The rest is tier drift - HT-only moles, strong/weak acid, electron-redox and bond-energy material asked of both tiers while the articles gate the same content - plus a unit-level gap: the separate-science Paper 1 content (transition metals in depth, nanoparticles, yield and atom economy, gas volumes, titrations, cells and fuel cells) is missing.
